title: Two flags at the Akal Takht
hookLine: two Nishan Sahibs stand there, for worldly and spiritual sovereignty, the spiritual one slightly higher

lines: A SAFFRON FLAG ABOVE THE ROOFTOPS.
cards: Drive through almost any town with Sikhs in it, from Punjab to Surrey to Yuba City, and look up. Above the rooftops there's a tall pole wrapped in saffron cloth, a triangular saffron flag at the top.
That's how you find the gurdwara. It's the Nishan Sahib, and every gurdwara flies one. But in Amritsar, at the Akal Takht, facing the Golden Temple, there are two, side by side.
Look closely: they aren't quite the same height. Today: two flags at the Akal Takht.

teach.b: Nishan means a sign, a mark; sahib is a word of honor. So the Nishan Sahib is the honored sign, the flag that says: here is a gurdwara, here you can find shelter and food. It carries the khanda, the Sikh emblem.

Akal means timeless, beyond death: one of the oldest names Sikhs use for God. Takht means throne. Guru Hargobind raised the Akal Takht in 1606, the same years he took up the two swords, right across from the Harmandir.
The Harmandir was the place of prayer; the Takht, where the community's worldly affairs were heard and decided. It's still the highest seat of Sikh authority.
Between them stand the two Nishan Sahibs, called by the names of Guru Hargobind's swords.

teach.h: MIRI AND PIRI, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Miri is worldly sovereignty: responsibility for justice, for the community, for the world as it is. Piri is spiritual sovereignty: the Name, prayer, the life of the soul.

teach.h: THE PIRI FLAG STANDS SLIGHTLY HIGHER.
teach.b: And the piri flag stands slightly higher. That's the whole lesson, written in the sky. The Sikh tradition doesn't ask its people to pick between the world and the spirit.
It raises both. But it doesn't pretend they're equal either. Worldly power is meant to answer to the spiritual; courage is meant to serve prayer, not the other way round.
Two poles, a short walk apart, and the difference in height is small enough to miss. That's fitting too. The spirit doesn't have to tower.
It just has to be a little higher.

how: Every gurdwara flies a Nishan Sahib, a saffron flag bearing the khanda; at the Akal Takht in Amritsar two stand side by side for miri and piri, and Sikhs bow toward the Akal Takht as the highest seat of Sikh authority.

o: a sweet treat shared after the evening prayers
spiritual sovereignty, the life of the soul
a song for weddings, with drums and dancing

games.q: the flags and the throne — tap the pairs.

s: the two flags at the Akal Takht are exactly the same height
the piri flag, for spiritual sovereignty, stands slightly higher.
every gurdwara flies a Nishan Sahib
the saffron flag with the khanda marks it as a place of shelter and food.
the Akal Takht was raised by Guru Hargobind
he raised it across from the Harmandir, as the seat where the community's affairs were decided.

games.q: you're raising two flags, one for worldly sovereignty and one for spiritual. how do you set them?
o: worldly higher, since that's where power sits.
only one flag; pick a side.
games.why: at the Akal Takht the piri flag stands a little higher. both raised, with worldly power answering to the spirit.

practice: If you can, stand up, feet under your hips, and let your spine grow tall like a flagpole, the crown of your head lifting a little higher, breathing easily for a minute.
Then sit, keep that little lift, and ask yourself: in my day, what's the higher flag?

wordCard.voice: Piri, spiritual sovereignty. The miri flag for worldly rule, the piri flag for the spirit, and the spiritual one a little higher.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nishan, a sign or banner; sahib, a word of honor.

carryVoice: Your line: spirit a little higher. Both flags fly; one just stands a bit taller. Day two hundred seventy-five, done.
